newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli economy takes unrest in stride.
newsitem.headline: Israeli economy takes unrest in stride.

text.p: Israel's economy seems to be shrugging off the potential fallout from government plans to build Jewish homes in Arab East Jerusalem, which has provoked international condemnation and Palestinian unrest.

Economists and market analysts said the Tel Aviv stock exchange was the main casualty from this latest crisis in the Middle East peace process but that consumer confidence, exports, tourism and inward investment looked relatively unscathed.

"I don't think consumers are buying less and exporters exporting less because of Har Homa. It's a temporary setback," said Gad Haker, head of the international department at Betucha Securities and Investments, echoing a widely held view.

Israeli-Palestinian tensions have risen in the last weeks with a Jordanian soldier killing seven Israeli schoolgirls, disputes over a West Bank troop redeployment by Israel and clashes over the planned Jewish settlement at Har Homa.
These events have had an immediate impact on the stock exchange, where the benchmark Mishtanim index has fallen nine percent since peaking on February 18.
"I think politics has had an impact -- less on valuations and fundamentals but more on sentiment. People are uncertain about recent events," said Betucha's Haker.
Overseas investors began buying heavily into Israeli equities earlier this year. But in the last three weeks they have stopped, causing local investors to hold back too.
"Local investors are worried about the foreign investors," said Haker. "They try to anticipate what they'll do."

The stock market may have suffered but economists were otherwise sanguine about the prospects of this latest crisis damaging the Israeli economy, which was already experiencing slower levels of growth.
"Certainly the peace process and the rate of its progress has influence on the economy and the market," said Hezy Gutman, chief economist at First International Bank of Israel.
"But the (economic) slowdown is minimally influenced by political developments," he added.

This was not the case last year, he said. A spate of bus bombings followed by Israeli attacks aimed at Hizbollah guerrillas in Lebanon helped snap a six-year string of fast growth as tourism plunged and Palestinian workers were barred from entering Israel.
Gutman estimated that security and political factors knocked one percent off economic growth in 1996 leaving it at 4.4 percent, versus 7.1 percent in 1995.
"In 1997, I don't see the security issues having the same level of impact," said Gutman, although he estimated growth would shrink to 3.5-4 percent this year for other reasons.

Israeli and foreign investors are generally inured to the twists and turns of the peace process. Last year foreigners pumped $2.59 billion in direct and financial investment into the economy, up 18 percent from 1995.

"Whoever wants to invest in this area has to expect that a bus could explode next week," said an investment banker who spoke on condition of anonymity. He said his clients were more concerned about the budget deficit and high interest rates.
Israel's politically sensitive tourism sector may feel the impact of security concerns this year, industry officials said.
But this would only become clear in another six to nine months as this was the time it took for tourists to make their holiday plans and book.
